issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The appraisal of permanent bodily damage is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma context. The other selected items consistently reflect ongoing external danger and hyperarousal (world dangerous, on guard, startle, false alarms, threat in silence) plus intrusive sensory memory, but there are no corroborating memory, threat, or strategy items indicating injury-focused trauma consequences, pain, disability, or body-related threat. For a refugee trauma profile, this isolated somatic-damage belief is not impossible, but in this item set it stands out as clinically incoherent with the dominant formulation of danger-based threat and avoidance.

vignette:
Liam is a 21-year-old public defender who came to the United States as a refugee from a war-torn region of Eastern Europe when he was seventeen. The trauma that continues to shape his life was not a single event but a sustained period of terror: the night his family's apartment was shelled, the long hours huddled in a basement while gunfire echoed through the streets, and the moment he saw a neighbor killed by shrapnel as they ran for cover. He remembers that neighbor's face, frozen in shock, more vividly than almost anything else-a picture that comes to him unbidden, often without warning. Sometimes, when these memories surface, he feels his body lock into the same crouched position he held in that basement, his muscles tensing as if the danger were still present. On other occasions, he will be sitting quietly at his desk reviewing case files and suddenly be flooded with the full, raw terror of that night, even though no clear image accompanies the feeling.

Liam has come to believe that the world is fundamentally dangerous, a conviction that has solidified over the past four years. He is certain that he must be on guard at all times, because you never know what could happen next. This hypervigilance is not a choice but a necessity he feels in his bones. As a public defender, he works in a chaotic courthouse where doors slam unexpectedly and voices rise in argument. In that environment, he has started to jump at ordinary sounds-the clatter of a filing cabinet, a sudden laugh from a colleague-that would not bother most people. He has also noticed that unusual silence, like the quiet that falls over the hallway before a hearing, makes him feel as if something dangerous is about to happen. He often reacts as if he is in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, his heart hammering and his palms sweating for no clear reason.

These moments of threat feed directly back into his memory. When he startles at a sound or feels that false alarm, the vivid images of the shelling and the neighbor's face often rush back with renewed intensity, as if the present moment has unlocked the past. And each time those memories return, they reinforce his belief that the world is unsafe-a cycle that has tightened over the months. To manage this, Liam has developed strategies that he believes keep him sane. He constantly monitors his own thoughts for signs that he might be going crazy, scanning his mind for any image or feeling that feels too overwhelming. He also avoids talking about the event or its aftermath with anyone, including his girlfriend, because he is certain that speaking about it will only make the memories worse or confirm that he is losing control. He avoids being reminded of the event by others, steering clear of news reports about refugees or war and leaving the room if a colleague mentions a similar story.

These strategies, however, have a cost. By not talking and by avoiding reminders, Liam never tests his belief that the world is dangerous. Instead, his avoidance reinforces his conviction that the threat is real and that his vigilance is necessary. He has started to feel more isolated from his girlfriend, who does not understand why he flinches when she touches his shoulder unexpectedly. At work, he has begun to turn down cases that involve violence, worried that the details will trigger him. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment in court last week: a door slammed, and he found himself on the floor, his hands over his head, before he even knew what had happened. He is afraid that he is losing control, and he is hoping that therapy can help him stop the cycle before it costs him his relationship and his career.
